title: History: how one ancient Koine became many modern dialects
lead: Greek has been written for about 3,500 years, and it has always had dialects. But the modern dialects are, with one or two exceptions, **not** the descendants of the ancient ones. Ancient Attic, Ionic, Doric and Aeolic were almost entirely replaced by a single common language, the Hellenistic **Κοινή**. The dialects you can hear today grew out of that Koine again, mostly between the 7th and 15th centuries AD, when wars, conquests and frontiers cut Greek-speaking regions off from one another. This page tells that story; the other pages show its results region by region.
facts: Modern dialects = Koine + about 1,000 years of separate development. Exceptions: **Tsakonian** (from Laconian Doric) and possibly the Greek of **southern Italy**.

Local varieties probably took shape between the 10th and 12th centuries, after earlier isolation in the 7th–10th (Arab raids). The first texts written in dialect come from Cyprus and Crete in the 14th century.
**διάλεκτος** = a strongly marked variety (Pontic, Tsakonian, Cappadocian, Italiot); **ιδίωμα** = a local variety close to the standard (most regional speech in Greece).
**Κοινή νεοελληνική** (Standard Modern Greek): spoken Demotic plus a large learned layer from Katharevousa; official in all schools since 1976.

sections.text:
The oldest Greek, the Mycenaean of the Linear B tablets (from about the 14th century BC), already shows dialect differences. After the Mycenaean palaces fell, Greek split freely into the dialects we know from inscriptions and literature: **Attic** (Athens), **Ionic** (the Aegean islands and the coast of Asia Minor), **Doric** (Sparta and Laconia, Argos, Corinth, Crete, Rhodes, and colonies such as Syracuse and Taranto), **Aeolic** (Lesbos, Thessaly, Boeotia), **Arcado-Cypriot** and **North-West Greek**. Colonists carried these dialects across the Mediterranean and the Black Sea, to southern Italy (**Μεγάλη Ελλάς**, Magna Graecia) and to towns such as Trapezous, today's Trabzon.

From the 5th century BC a levelling process began. The dialects of the city-states lost ground to an **Attic-Ionic Κοινή**, and Alexander's conquests and the Hellenistic kingdoms spread that Koine from Egypt to Afghanistan. Under Roman rule it became the common language of the whole eastern Mediterranean, the language of the New Testament. By late antiquity the old dialects had died out almost everywhere. The one clear survivor is the speech of Laconia, which lives on as **Tsakonian**.

examples.en: 'day': Attic and Koine have η where Doric kept the old long ā. The modern standard continues the Koine form; Tsakonian keeps the Doric α in many words (α μάτη 'the mother', from Doric μάτηρ).
'daughter': lost in the standard, but alive in Tsakonian as α σάτη (θ > σ, a Laconian trait).

sections.h: 2. Koine Greek and the birth of diglossia
sections.text:
The Koine kept changing in speech. Vowel length was lost, the pitch accent became a stress accent, ancient **υ, οι, η, ει** gradually merged with **ι** (the change called iotacism, **ιωτακισμός**), **β, γ, δ** became fricatives, and the dative case began to retreat. Many grammar points you learn today (the stress accent, **θα** futures, **να** in place of the infinitive) are the end result of these Koine and Byzantine changes.

From the 1st century BC writers who admired classical Athens (the **Atticists**) refused to write the Koine as it was spoken and imitated 5th-century Attic instead. From then on, Greek had two layers: a natural spoken language and an archaising written one. Linguists call this **διγλωσσία** (diglossia). It lasted, in one form or another, until 1976.

sections.h: 3. Byzantium: frontiers, raids and the first splits
sections.text: The modern dialect map started to form when parts of the Greek-speaking world were cut off from Constantinople. Scholars cannot follow the process in detail, because people wrote in learned Greek, not in their local speech. What is known points to long periods of isolation.

timeline.text: Slavic groups settle across much of the Balkans and the Peloponnese. Greek is later restored there, but the old local continuity is broken in many places.

Arab raids. **Cyprus** is shared between Byzantium and the Caliphate from the late 7th century until 965. The **Pontus** is a frontier zone. The **Dodecanese** are long a no man's land between Byzantium and the Arabs. These isolated centuries are where scholars place the start of Cypriot, Pontic and Dodecanesian distinctiveness.
**Crete** is an Arab emirate, out of contact with the rest of the Greek world, until Nikephoros Phokas retakes it.
Byzantine defeat at Manzikert. Seljuk Turks take central Anatolia, and **Cappadocia** is cut off from the Greek world. Cappadocian develops under Turkish influence from here on.
The period when, many scholars think, the main local varieties were formed out of Medieval Greek.

sections.h: 4. Latin rule: Venetians, Franks and Lusignans
sections.text: After the Fourth Crusade took Constantinople in **1204**, much of the Greek world passed to Latin rulers. Where Greek was no longer the language of a Byzantine court and church administration, people began to **write their own dialect**: the first dialect texts come from these Latin-ruled areas. Italian (above all Venetian) and Old French words entered the local speech, which is why island dialects are full of Romance loans that the mainland lacks.

timeline.text: **Cyprus** under the Lusignan kings. Legal texts (the Assizes, 14th c.) and the chronicle of Leontios Machairas (15th c.) are written in Cypriot. Old French loanwords enter the dialect.
The **Empire of Trebizond** rules the Pontic coast, independent of Constantinople, until the Ottomans take it in 1461.
**Crete** under Venice. The Cretan Renaissance (16th–17th c.) produces drama and poetry in Cretan dialect, above all Kornaros's **Ερωτόκριτος** (c. 1600).
Venetian and other Latin lords in the **Cyclades** (the Duchy of the Archipelago at Naxos). Catholic communities on Syros, Tinos and Naxos; Italian loans in the island dialects.
**Corfu** under Venice (the other Ionian Islands from the 15th–16th c.). The Ionian Islands largely escape Ottoman rule; Italian is the language of the elite.

Albanian-speaking (Arvanite) settlers fill much of Attica, Boeotia, southern Euboea and the Peloponnese. Greek survives in pockets such as Athens, Megara, Aegina and Kymi, the later **Old Athenian** group.

sections.text:
Constantinople fell in **1453**; Trebizond in 1461; Rhodes in 1522; Cyprus in 1571; Crete in 1669. For three to four centuries most Greek speakers lived in the Ottoman Empire, where the Orthodox Church, not the language, defined who was 'Greek' (**Ρωμιός**, from Byzantine 'Roman'). That is why speakers of Pontic call their language **Ρωμαίικα** and why many Orthodox Christians in central Anatolia spoke Turkish (Karamanli Turkish, written in Greek letters).

Turkish loanwords entered every dialect, especially in vocabulary for food, crafts, clothes and administration (**καφές, τζάμι, μπογιά, κιόσκι, χαλάλι**). In the interior of Asia Minor the influence went much further, into sounds and grammar, as Cappadocian shows. The written language stayed archaising: the Church and the educated Phanariot families of Constantinople used a learned Greek with essentially modern syntax.

sections.h: 6. The new state and the Language Question
sections.text:
When the Greek state was founded (independence won 1821–1830, Athens capital from 1834), it needed a national language. Two answers competed. **Καθαρεύουσα** ('the purifying one'), shaped by Adamantios Korais's 'middle way', kept modern syntax but restored ancient words and endings; it became the language of the state, schools, church and press. **Δημοτική** ('the people's language') was the spoken language; poets such as Dionysios Solomos (from Zakynthos) wrote in it, and Yannis Psycharis's book **Το ταξίδι μου** (1888) made its use a cause.

The spoken standard itself formed in Athens, where people from every region met. Since the old local Athenian dialect was already giving way, the new urban speech levelled the regional differences. Its base is southern: it has southern vowels, the genitive (not accusative) for indirect objects, and grammar close to that of the Peloponnese and the Ionian Islands, though recent research argues that the Peloponnesian dialects may look standard partly because they converged early on Athenian speech, rather than the other way round. The fight over the two forms lasted through the 20th century and was settled after the fall of the junta: **Law 309/1976** made Demotic the language of education and of the state, and the **monotonic** accent system followed in **1982**. Today's standard is Demotic with a large learned layer taken from Katharevousa (words such as **επιπλέον, εντούτοις, υπό, εν τω μεταξύ**).

examples.el: Καθαρεύουσα: Ο οίκος ούτος ανήκει εις τον πατέρα μου.
examples.std: Αυτό το σπίτι ανήκει στον πατέρα μου.
examples.en: This house belongs to my father: the same sentence in purist and standard form.

sections.h: 7. 1923: the population exchange and the end of the old map
sections.text:
The Balkan Wars (1912–13) added Macedonia, Epirus, Crete and the North Aegean islands to Greece. Then came the Greco-Turkish war and the Asia Minor Catastrophe of 1922. The **Convention of Lausanne** (30 January 1923) ordered a compulsory exchange: about 1.2 million Orthodox Christians left Anatolia and Eastern Thrace for Greece, and about 400,000 Muslims left Greece for Turkey. Religion, not language, decided who moved: Turkish-speaking Christians came to Greece, and Greek-speaking Muslims (Cretan Muslims, some Pontic speakers) went to Turkey or stayed there.

For the dialects this was decisive. Pontic, Cappadocian, Pharasiot, Silliot, Smyrniot and the Greek of Constantinople's hinterland lost their homelands. Refugees were settled in Macedonia, Thrace and around Athens, where the next generations shifted to the standard. Only Pontic still has large numbers of speakers. The Greek of Istanbul survived among the community exempted from the exchange, now very small.
notes: **Smyrna** (İzmir) had an urban Greek with French and Italian loans and some local forms of the article; it is not one of Trudgill's dialects with the six key features (see the classification page).
**Constantinopolitan Greek** (**Πολίτικα**) is close to the standard but has its own loans (Turkish, French, Italian), a dark **λ**, and semi-northern vowel loss.
**Dodecanese**: Italian rule 1912–1943; joined to Greece by the 1947 Treaty of Paris (formally 1948).
**Cyprus**: British 1878–1960, independent since 1960; Cypriot Greek coexists with Standard Greek and English.

sections.text: Radio, television, schooling and migration to the cities have shrunk most dialects to an accent, a few words and some grammar habits. Cypriot is the exception: it is everyone's everyday language on the island. Cretan is vigorous in speech and song. Pontic lives on in families, associations and music, and as Romeyka in a few valleys of north-east Turkey. Tsakonian, Griko and Greko, and Cappadocian are severely endangered, with revival efforts in schools and online. When a Greek friend says **«Ίντα κάνεις;»**, **«Είντα λες;»** or **«Σε είπα!»**, you are hearing the history told on these pages.

questions.q: Most modern Greek dialects descend from…
options: the ancient dialects of each region
questions.why: Ancient dialects were almost all replaced by the Koine; modern dialects formed from it again in Byzantine times. Tsakonian (and possibly Italiot) are the exceptions.

questions.q: Which modern variety continues ancient Laconian Doric?
questions.why: Tsakonian keeps Doric traits such as α for Attic η (α μάτη) and the Laconian change of θ to σ.

questions.q: Why did the first texts written in dialect appear in Cyprus and Crete?
options: They were ruled by Latin powers, outside Byzantine learned culture
They had no Greek schools at all
questions.answer: They were ruled by Latin powers, outside Byzantine learned culture
questions.why: Under the Lusignans (Cyprus) and Venice (Crete), Greek had no imperial learned standard to follow, so legal texts, chronicles and poetry were written in local speech.

questions.q: What decided who moved in the 1923 population exchange?
questions.why: Orthodox Christians went to Greece and Muslims to Turkey, whatever language they spoke.

questions.q: When did Demotic become the language of Greek schools and the state?
questions.why: Law 309/1976, after the fall of the junta; the monotonic system followed in 1982.

gloss.Κοινή: Κοινή — the Hellenistic 'common' Greek (4th c. BC – 6th c. AD)
gloss.κοινή: κοινή — common; η κοινή νεοελληνική = Standard Modern Greek
gloss.ιδίωμα: ιδίωμα — local variety, idiom (less divergent than a διάλεκτος)
gloss.Καθαρεύουσα: καθαρεύουσα — 'the purifying one': the learned written Greek of 1830–1976
gloss.διγλωσσία: διγλωσσία — diglossia: a high written and a low spoken variety side by side
gloss.ιωτακισμός: ιωτακισμός — iotacism: η, ι, υ, ει, οι all pronounced [i]
gloss.Ρωμιός: Ρωμιός — Greek (Orthodox), lit. 'Roman', the Byzantine self-name
gloss.Ρωμαίικα: ρωμαίικα — Greek, lit. 'Roman (language)'; Pontic speakers' name for their dialect
gloss.Μεγάλη: μεγάλος — great; Μεγάλη Ελλάς = Magna Graecia, the Greek colonies of southern Italy
gloss.Σε: σε — you (acc.); northern «σε είπα» = standard «σου είπα» 'I told you'
gloss.εις: εις — to, in (Katharevousa form of σε)
